title: Underpromotion
line: When a knight or a rook is better than a queen.

steps.text: The Saavedra position: White's pawn is about to promote, and Black's rook checks the king away first.
Promote, but not to a queen. Make a rook.

wrong.c7c8q: Then the rook checks from c4. If your queen takes it, Black has no move at all: stalemate.

steps.hint: A queen would let Black give up the rook for a stalemate.
steps.after: Black can no longer give the rook away for a stalemate.

steps.text: Step your king next to the black rook. Now it is attacked, and your rook threatens mate.
steps.after: Black cannot save the rook and stop the mate at once.

steps.text: A knight can be better too: it jumps where a queen cannot, and can give check and attack the queen at once.
Promote to a knight, with check and an attack on the queen.
steps.hint: A knight on the last row would attack the king and the queen.
steps.after: Check, and the queen is forked.
The pawn became a knight, and the knight took the queen.

summary: A queen is not always best. A rook can avoid stalemate, and a knight can give check and fork at once.
